## program

A file is one module; the entry module has a main function.

- A file holds exactly one defmodule with an uppercase name.
- The entry module has exactly one main/0; imported modules have none.
- alchem build main.alc compiles to a native executable; alchem check only reports errors.
- The whole file is type-checked before anything runs, including unused functions.

Example: a complete program

```elixir
defmodule Hello do
  def greeting(name: string): string do
    "hello, #{name}"
  end

  def main() do
    IO.puts(greeting("world"))
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax functions, alchem syntax modules, alchem syntax tests

## values

Integers, floats, booleans and strings.

- integer is signed 64-bit and overflow fails at run time; float is 64-bit.
- A float literal needs digits on both sides of the point: 1.0, not 1.
- There is no implicit conversion: 1 + 1.5 is a type error. Use Float.from_integer, round, trunc.
- A float in interpolation or to_string is its shortest text, in exponent form when that is shorter: 1000.0 is "1.0e3" and 1250.0 is "1250.0". inspect keeps plain digits.
- There is no nil: use option and result. Atoms are a type of their own (see atoms).

Example: literals

```elixir
count = 42
price = 9.5
ready = true
name = "ada"
assert(count + 1 == 43)
assert(price * 2.0 == 19.0)
assert(ready and name == "ada")
assert(Float.from_integer(count) + 0.5 == 42.5)
```

See also: alchem syntax operators, alchem syntax strings, alchem syntax option-result

## bindings

name = expression binds a name once; bindings are immutable.

- A name cannot be rebound or shadowed in the same function: pick a new name.
- An annotation gives the type where the value alone does not: xs: list[integer] = [].
- Bindings made inside a branch do not escape it.
- The left side may be a pattern (see patterns).

Example: bindings and annotations

```elixir
total = 2 + 3 * 4
doubled = total * 2
empty: list[string] = []
missing: option[integer] = none
assert(doubled == 28)
assert(length(empty) == 0)
assert(missing == none)
```

See also: alchem syntax patterns, alchem syntax values

## operators

Arithmetic, comparison, boolean, string and list operators.

- Arithmetic: + - * / on two integers or two floats; integer / truncates; % and rem are integer remainder; ** is power.
- Comparison: == != < <= > >=. == compares lists, tuples, maps, structs and sum types structurally.
- Boolean: and, or, not (also && || !); operands must be booleans.
- Strings: <> concatenates; text =~ ~r/pattern/ tests a regular expression.
- Lists: ++ concatenates, -- removes, value in enumerable tests membership.
- first..last is an inclusive range; first..last//step sets the step.
- |> passes the left value as the first argument of the call on the right.

Example: operators

```elixir
assert(7 / 2 == 3 and 7 % 2 == 1)
assert(2 ** 10 == 1024)
assert(7.0 / 2.0 == 3.5)
assert("al" <> "chem" == "alchem")
assert([1, 2] ++ [3] == [1, 2, 3])
assert([1, 2, 3, 2] -- [2] == [1, 3, 2])
assert(2 in [1, 2, 3] and not (5 in 1..3))
assert("order 42" =~ ~r/\d+/)
assert({1, "a"} == {1, "a"})
```

See also: alchem syntax pipes, alchem syntax ranges, alchem syntax strings

## strings

UTF-8 text with interpolation, heredocs and the String module.

- "#{expression}" interpolates a string, integer, float or boolean; write \#{ for the literal characters.
- A heredoc starts with """ at the end of a line and ends with """ on its own line; the closing line's indentation is removed from every line.
- A heredoc has escapes and #{...} interpolation, as a string does; ~S""" starts one that is taken literally, as documentation with examples usually is.
- inspect(value) renders any value as text; to_string renders the four primitive types.

Example: interpolation and concatenation

```elixir
name = "ada"
age = 36
line = "#{name} is #{age}"
assert(line == "ada is 36")
assert(String.upcase(name) <> "!" == "ADA!")
assert(inspect([1, 2]) == "[1, 2]")
```

Example: heredoc

```elixir
text = """
  first line
    indented
  """
assert(text == "first line\n  indented\n")
```

See also: alchem syntax sigils, alchem doc String, alchem doc Regex

## comments

# comments, and @moduledoc, @doc and @typedoc documentation.

- # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.
- @moduledoc documents the module, @doc the next function, @typedoc the next struct or type. Each takes a string or heredoc.
- alx> lines inside @doc are examples; a test file runs them with doctest Module (see doctests).
- alchem doc file.alc prints a file's documentation.

Example: a documented module

```elixir
defmodule Temperature do
  @moduledoc """
  Temperature conversion.
  """

  @doc """
  Converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.

      alx> Temperature.to_fahrenheit(100.0)
      212.0
  """
  def to_fahrenheit(celsius: float): float do
    # nine fifths, plus the offset
    celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
  end

  def main() do
    assert(to_fahrenheit(0.0) == 32.0)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax doctests, alchem syntax strings

## functions

def name(parameter: type): result do ... end.

- Parameters carry types; the result type follows the parentheses and may be left out when a first clause or the body fixes it.
- The last expression is the result; return value leaves early.
- defp defines a function private to its module.
- A function that returns nothing omits the result type.
- Names may end in ? or !. Recursion is the loop; Process.loop and Enum cover the rest.
- &name refers to a named function as a value.
- name: type \\ value gives a trailing parameter a default, which a call may leave out. The value is a constant: literals, lists, tuples and maps of them, none, some(...), ok(...) or error(...).
- A function has one number of parameters: there is no second definition with a different arity.

Example: definitions and calls

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def area(width: float, height: float): float do
    width * height
  end

  def sign(n: integer): string do
    if n < 0 do
      return "negative"
    end
    "non-negative"
  end

  defp double(n: integer): integer do
    n * 2
  end

  def main() do
    assert(area(2.0, 3.0) == 6.0)
    assert(sign(-1) == "negative")
    assert(Enum.map([1, 2], &double) == [2, 4])
  end
end
```

Example: default arguments

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def greet(name: string, greeting: string \\ "hello", marks: integer \\ 1): string do
    "#{greeting}, #{name}" <> String.duplicate("!", marks)
  end

  def main() do
    assert(greet("ada") == "hello, ada!")
    assert(greet("ada", "hi") == "hi, ada!")
    assert(greet("ada", "hi", 3) == "hi, ada!!!")
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax clauses, alchem syntax anonymous-functions, alchem syntax generics

## clauses

Several definitions of one function, chosen by pattern and guard.

- Clauses are tried top to bottom; parameters may be patterns and literals.
- The first clause gives the types; later clauses may leave them out.
- when adds a guard, a boolean expression over the parameters.
- Clauses of one function must be adjacent and have the same number of parameters; a definition with another number of parameters is another function, as in Elixir: area/1 and area/2.
- Together the clauses must cover every input: end with a catch-all when guards leave gaps.

Example: pattern-matching clauses

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def fact(0): integer do
    1
  end

  def fact(n: integer) when n > 0 do
    n * fact(n - 1)
  end

  def fact(_) do
    raise("fact needs a non-negative number")
  end

  def sum([]: list[integer]): integer do
    0
  end

  def sum([head | tail]) do
    head + sum(tail)
  end

  def main() do
    assert(fact(5) == 120)
    assert(sum([1, 2, 3]) == 6)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax patterns, alchem syntax functions

## anonymous-functions

fn x -> body end, captures with &, and closures.

- fn x, y -> body end takes its types from where it is used: an argument, an annotated binding or a return.
- Where nothing gives the types, annotate: fn(x: integer): integer do x + 1 end.
- &(&1 + &2) and &String.length(&1) are short forms; &name refers to a named function.
- A parameter may be a pattern: fn {key, value} -> ... end.
- With clauses on the lines after fn, each pattern -> body with an optional guard, the function takes one argument and tries them in order; match a tuple for several values.
- A function value is called like a function, f(1), or as in Elixir, f.(1). Its type is fn[argument, ..., result].
- Functions capture the bindings around them, which never change.

Example: function values

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def adder(offset: integer): fn[integer, integer] do
    fn value -> value + offset end
  end

  def main() do
    add_ten = adder(10)
    assert(add_ten(5) == 15)
    assert(Enum.map([1, 2, 3], fn n -> n * n end) == [1, 4, 9])
    assert(Enum.reduce([1, 2, 3], 0, &(&1 + &2)) == 6)
    assert(Enum.map(["a", "bb"], &String.length(&1)) == [1, 2])
    square = fn(n: integer): integer do n * n end
    assert(square(4) == 16)
    pairs = Enum.map(%{"a" => 1}, fn {key, value} -> "#{key}:#{value}" end)
    assert(pairs == ["a:1"])
  end
end
```

Example: clauses

```elixir
labels = Enum.map([0, -3, 7], fn
  0 -> "zero"
  n when n < 0 -> "negative"
  _ -> "positive"
end)
assert(labels == ["zero", "negative", "positive"])
areas = Enum.map([{2, 3}, {4, 0}], fn
  {_, 0} -> 0
  {width, height} -> width * height
end)
assert(areas == [6, 0])
```

See also: alchem syntax functions, alchem doc Enum

## generics

Lowercase type names are type variables.

- A function is generic in the type variables of its parameters; each call picks the types.
- Inside the function a type variable's values can be passed, stored, returned and compared, but not used in arithmetic.
- Structs and sum types take parameters in brackets: struct Pair[a, b], type Tree[t].
- A misspelled type name is therefore read as a type variable and reported where the value is first used.

Example: a generic function and type

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  struct Pair[a, b] do
    left: a
    right: b
  end

  def swap(pair: Pair[a, b]): Pair[b, a] do
    %Pair{left: pair.right, right: pair.left}
  end

  def first_or(items: list[t], fallback: t): t do
    case items do
      [] -> fallback
      [head | _] -> head
    end
  end

  def main() do
    swapped = swap(%Pair{left: 1, right: "one"})
    assert(swapped.left == "one" and swapped.right == 1)
    assert(first_or(["a"], "z") == "a")
    assert(first_or(Enum.take([1], 0), 9) == 9)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax functions, alchem syntax structs, alchem syntax sum-types

## if

if condition do ... else ... end, as a statement or a value.

- The condition must be a boolean; there is no truthiness.
- As a value both branches must end in the same type, and else is required.
- There is no else if: nest, or use cond.
- unless condition do ... end runs its body when the condition is false; it may have an else and be used as a value.

Example: statement and value

```elixir
count = 3
label = if count > 0 do "some" else "none" end
assert(label == "some")
if count > 2 do
  IO.puts("many")
else
  IO.puts("few")
end
```

Example: unless

```elixir
items = [1, 2]
unless items == [] do
  IO.puts("has items")
end
state = unless length(items) > 5 do "short" else "long" end
assert(state == "short")
```

See also: alchem syntax cond, alchem syntax case

## case

Matches a value against patterns, with optional guards.

- Arms are pattern -> body, tried in order; _ matches anything.
- when adds a guard to an arm.
- A case over a sum type, option or result must cover every variant or end in a catch-all.
- As a value every arm must end in the same type.

Example: matching lists, tuples and results

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def describe(items: list[integer]): string do
    case items do
      [] -> "empty"
      [only] -> "one: #{only}"
      [first | _] when first < 0 -> "starts negative"
      _ -> "many"
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(describe([7]) == "one: 7")
    assert(describe([-1, 2]) == "starts negative")
    parsed = case Integer.parse("42") do
      ok(n) -> n
      error(_) -> 0
    end
    assert(parsed == 42)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax patterns, alchem syntax sum-types, alchem syntax option-result

## cond

Runs the first branch whose condition is true.

- Arms are condition -> body; end with true -> for the default.
- Without a default, a cond in which nothing is true fails with no cond clause matched.

Example: cond as a value

```elixir
n = 0
label = cond do
  n < 0 -> "negative"
  n == 0 -> "zero"
  true -> "positive"
end
assert(label == "zero")
```

See also: alchem syntax if, alchem syntax case

## patterns

Destructuring in bindings, case arms, function parameters, fn parameters, with and for.

- Tuples {a, b}; lists [], [a, b], [head | tail]; maps %{"key" => value}; structs %Name{field: value}; sum variants Shape.circle(r); some(x), none, ok(x), error(e).
- Literals match themselves; _ ignores; ^name matches the value of an existing binding instead of binding.
- A map or struct pattern matches when the listed keys or fields match; others are ignored.
- A binding whose pattern does not match fails with pattern match failed.

Example: destructuring

```elixir
{count, label} = {3, "ok"}
[first | rest] = [1, 2, 3]
assert(count == 3 and label == "ok")
assert(first == 1 and rest == [2, 3])
expected = 3
matched = case {3, "x"} do
  {^expected, text} -> text
  _ -> "other"
end
assert(matched == "x")
found = case %{"count" => 4} do
  %{"count" => n} when n > 0 -> n
  _ -> 0
end
assert(found == 4)
```

See also: alchem syntax case, alchem syntax clauses, alchem syntax with, alchem syntax for

## pipes

value |> function(arguments) passes the value as the first argument.

- Each step is a call; the piped value becomes its first argument.
- then(value, fn) pipes into a function value; tap(value, fn) runs an effect and passes the value on.

Example: a pipeline

```elixir
total = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
  |> Enum.filter(&(rem(&1, 2) == 0))
  |> Enum.map(&(&1 * &1))
  |> Enum.sum()
assert(total == 56)
assert(("  alchem  " |> String.trim() |> String.upcase()) == "ALCHEM")
```

See also: alchem doc Enum, alchem doc Stream

## with

Chains pattern matches, stopping at the first that fails.

- Each clause is pattern <- expression; bindings are visible to later clauses and the body.
- Without else, the first value that does not match becomes the result, so error(reason) and none pass straight through.
- With else, that value is matched against the else arms.

Example: chaining results

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def parse_point(text: string): result[tuple[integer, integer], string] do
    with [left, right] <- String.split(text, ","),
         ok(x) <- Integer.parse(left),
         ok(y) <- Integer.parse(right) do
      ok({x, y})
    else
      error(reason) -> error("bad number: #{reason}")
      parts -> error("expected 2 parts, got #{length(parts)}")
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(parse_point("3,4") == ok({3, 4}))
    assert(parse_point("3") == error("expected 2 parts, got 1"))
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax option-result, alchem syntax patterns, alchem syntax try

## for

Comprehensions: generators and filters producing a list.

- for pattern <- enumerable, filter, do: expression — or a do ... end block.
- Several generators nest; later ones see earlier bindings.
- Elements that do not match a generator's pattern are skipped.
- Without an option the result is a list. A body that ends in IO.puts or another call with no value gives {} for each element, as Elixir's gives :ok. One option may follow the generators and filters.
- into: collectable adds the values to a map (from {key, value} tuples), a set, a list or a string; an empty %{} or [] takes its type from the values.
- uniq: true drops values already produced.
- reduce: initial takes a do block of accumulator -> body arms; the body's value is the next accumulator and the last one is the result. An empty initial value such as %{} needs a type from an annotation.

Example: generators and filters

```elixir
squares = for n <- 1..5, do: n * n
assert(squares == [1, 4, 9, 16, 25])
pairs = for x <- [1, 2, 3], y <- [1, 2, 3], x < y do
  {x, y}
end
assert(pairs == [{1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}])
present = for some(n) <- [some(1), none, some(3)], do: n
assert(present == [1, 3])
```

Example: into, uniq and reduce

```elixir
squares = for n <- 1..3, into: %{}, do: {n, n * n}
assert(squares == %{1 => 1, 2 => 4, 3 => 9})
initials = for word <- ["bee", "ant", "bat"], uniq: true, do: String.slice(word, 0, 1)
assert(initials == ["b", "a"])
total = for x <- [1, 2, 3], x != 2, reduce: 0 do
  acc -> acc + x
end
assert(total == 4)
counts: map[string, integer] = for word <- ["a", "b", "a"], reduce: %{} do
  seen -> Map.update(seen, word, 1, &(&1 + 1))
end
assert(counts == %{"a" => 2, "b" => 1})
```

See also: alchem syntax ranges, alchem syntax patterns, alchem doc Enum

## try

try / rescue / catch / else / after, raise, throw and defexception.

- raise(message) fails the current process with a message; every runtime failure has one.
- defexception Name do message: string ... end declares an exception, a struct with a message field; raise(%Name{...}) raises it.
- rescue arms match a failure: e in Name binds the exception, %Name{field: x} matches its fields, and a string literal or a name matches the message of any failure.
- throw(value) unwinds to the nearest catch arm that takes the value's type; the type comes from the throws in the body, from the arm's pattern, or from value: Type ->.
- else arms match the body's value when nothing was raised or thrown; a failure in an else arm is not rescued by the same try.
- after runs on every way out; its value is discarded. return cannot be used inside try.
- Prefer result and option for expected failures; try is for the unexpected, and throw for leaving a loop early.

Example: rescuing a failure

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def safe_div(a: integer, b: integer): result[integer, string] do
    try do
      ok(a / b)
    rescue
      "division by zero" -> error("cannot divide by zero")
      message -> error(message)
    after
      IO.puts("divided")
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(safe_div(6, 3) == ok(2))
    assert(safe_div(1, 0) == error("cannot divide by zero"))
    message = try do
      raise("boom")
    rescue
      text -> text
    end
    assert(message == "boom")
  end
end
```

Example: exceptions, throw and else

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  defexception NotFound do
    message: string
    id: integer
  end

  def fetch(id: integer): string do
    if id > 9 do
      raise(%NotFound{message: "no such item", id: id})
    end
    "item"
  end

  def main() do
    missing = try do
      fetch(42)
    rescue
      e in NotFound -> "missing " <> to_string(e.id)
    end
    assert(missing == "missing 42")
    first = try do
      Enum.each([1, 7, 9], fn n -> if n > 5 do throw(n) end end)
      0
    catch
      n -> n
    end
    assert(first == 7)
    parsed = try do
      Integer.parse("12")
    rescue
      _ -> 0
    else
      ok(n) -> n
      error(_) -> -1
    end
    assert(parsed == 12)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax option-result, alchem syntax with

## lists

list[T]: immutable, written [1, 2, 3].

- An empty list needs a type from an annotation or its use: xs: list[integer] = [].
- [head | tail] is a pattern; build with prepend(list, value), ++ or Enum.
- list[index] reads by zero-based position and fails out of range; Enum.at returns an option.
- length(list), hd(list), tl(list). The Enum module works on every enumerable; List has positional updates.

Example: building and reading lists

```elixir
numbers = [3, 1, 2]
assert(numbers[0] == 3 and length(numbers) == 3)
assert(prepend(numbers, 0) == [0, 3, 1, 2])
assert(Enum.sort(numbers) == [1, 2, 3])
assert(Enum.at(numbers, 9) == none)
nested: list[list[integer]] = [[], [1, 2]]
assert(nested[1][0] == 1)
```

See also: alchem syntax for, alchem syntax patterns, alchem doc Enum, alchem doc List

## tuples

tuple[A, B]: a fixed group of values, written {a, b}.

- Positions have their own types; read with tuple[index] using a literal index, or destructure.
- {} is the empty tuple, the value of a function that returns nothing useful.

Example: tuples

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def min_max(items: list[integer]): tuple[integer, integer] do
    {Enum.min(items), Enum.max(items)}
  end

  def main() do
    {low, high} = min_max([3, 9, 2])
    assert(low == 2 and high == 9)
    pair = {"a", 1}
    assert(pair[0] == "a" and pair[1] == 1)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax patterns, alchem syntax structs

## maps

map[K, V]: immutable, written %{key => value}.

- Keys are integers, strings or booleans; all keys share one type and all values another.
- map[key] fails when the key is absent; Map.get returns an option, or a default with a third argument.
- Map.put, Map.delete, Map.update and friends return a new map; the original is unchanged.
- Maps enumerate as {key, value} tuples in ascending key order.
- An empty map needs a type: counts: map[string, integer] = %{}.

Example: reading and updating maps

```elixir
stock = %{"apple" => 3, "pear" => 0}
more = Map.put(stock, "fig", 7)
assert(stock["apple"] == 3 and map_size(more) == 3)
assert(Map.get(stock, "kiwi") == none)
assert(Map.get(stock, "kiwi", 0) == 0)
assert(Map.update(stock, "apple", 1, &(&1 + 1))["apple"] == 4)
names = Enum.map(stock, fn {name, _} -> name end)
assert(names == ["apple", "pear"])
counts: map[string, integer] = %{}
assert(map_size(counts) == 0)
```

See also: alchem syntax structs, alchem doc Map, alchem doc MapSet

## structs

struct Name do field: type ... end: a named record.

- Declared inside a module. A field may have a default, field: type = value, which %Name{...} fills in when it leaves the field out; every other field must be given.
- value.field reads; %Name{value | field: new} copies with fields replaced.
- %Name{field: pattern} is a pattern; unlisted fields are ignored.
- From another module the type is Module.Name and the literal %Module.Name{...}.

Example: declare, build, update, match

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  struct Account do
    owner: string
    balance: integer = 0
  end

  def deposit(account: Account, amount: integer): Account do
    %Account{account | balance: account.balance + amount}
  end

  def owner_of(%Account{owner: name}: Account): string do
    name
  end

  def main() do
    assert(%Account{owner: "bo"}.balance == 0)
    account = %Account{owner: "ada", balance: 10}
    richer = deposit(account, 15)
    assert(richer.balance == 25 and account.balance == 10)
    assert(owner_of(richer) == "ada")
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax sum-types, alchem syntax generics, alchem syntax patterns

## sum-types

type Name do variant(fields) ... end: a value that is one of several shapes.

- Build with Name.variant(arguments), or Name.variant for one without fields; the same forms are patterns.
- A case or set of clauses over a sum type must cover every variant or include a catch-all.
- Sum types may be recursive and take type parameters: type Tree[t].
- Use a sum type where Elixir would use atoms or tagged tuples.

Example: variants and matching

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  type Shape do
    circle(radius: float)
    rect(width: float, height: float)
    empty
  end

  def area(shape: Shape): float do
    case shape do
      Shape.circle(radius) -> 3.14159 * radius * radius
      Shape.rect(width, height) -> width * height
      Shape.empty -> 0.0
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(area(Shape.rect(2.0, 3.0)) == 6.0)
    assert(area(Shape.empty) == 0.0)
    shapes = [Shape.circle(1.0), Shape.empty]
    assert(length(shapes) == 2)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax case, alchem syntax structs, alchem syntax option-result

## option-result

option[T] is some(value) or none; result[T, E] is ok(value) or error(reason).

- These replace nil and {:ok, value} / {:error, reason} tuples.
- Library functions return option for an absent value and result for an expected failure; names ending in ! fail instead.
- Take them apart with case, with, or a pattern in for.
- none, or ok(1) alone, needs a type from an annotation, parameter or return type.

Example: returning and matching

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def halve(n: integer): result[integer, string] do
    if n % 2 == 0 do
      ok(n / 2)
    else
      error("#{n} is odd")
    end
  end

  def first_even(items: list[integer]): option[integer] do
    Enum.find(items, &(rem(&1, 2) == 0))
  end

  def main() do
    assert(halve(10) == ok(5))
    assert(halve(3) == error("3 is odd"))
    label = case first_even([1, 3]) do
      some(n) -> "found #{n}"
      none -> "none found"
    end
    assert(label == "none found")
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax case, alchem syntax with, alchem syntax try

## atoms

:name is an atom; [name: value] is a keyword list.

- An atom is a name used as a value, of type atom. Atoms compare, sort, match in patterns, key maps and interpolate as their name.
- A colon starts an atom unless it follows a name or a closing bracket, where it introduces a type or a value: write a space before :name.
- Any atom fits the type atom, so a case over atoms needs a catch-all. For a fixed set of alternatives the compiler should check, use a sum type.
- Library functions do not return {:ok, value} tuples: they return option and result.
- [name: value, other: value] is a keyword list, a list[tuple[atom, T]] whose values share one type. It keeps its order and may repeat a key; the Keyword module reads and changes it.

Example: atoms and a keyword list

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def status(code: integer): atom do
    case code do
      200 -> :ok
      404 -> :not_found
      _ -> :error
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(status(404) == :not_found)
    assert("status: #{status(200)}" == "status: ok")
    counts = %{:red => 1, :blue => 2}
    assert(counts[:blue] == 2)
    options = [verbose: true, color: false]
    assert(Keyword.get(options, :verbose) == some(true))
    assert(Keyword.put(options, :color, true) == [color: true, verbose: true])
    assert(options == [{:verbose, true}, {:color, false}])
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax sum-types, alchem syntax option-result, alchem syntax maps, alchem doc Atom, alchem doc Keyword

## ranges

first..last: the integers from first to last inclusive.

- Counts down when first > last; first..last//step sets the step.
- A range is a Range struct, with first, last and step, and an enumerable of its integers: use it with Enum, Stream, for and in, and the Range functions. Written where a stream[integer] is expected, it is that stream.

Example: ranges

```elixir
assert(Enum.to_list(1..4) == [1, 2, 3, 4])
assert(Enum.to_list(3..1) == [3, 2, 1])
assert(Enum.to_list(0..10//5) == [0, 5, 10])
assert(Enum.sum(1..100) == 5050)
assert(3 in 1..5)
r = 1..10//3
assert(r.step == 3 and Range.size(r) == 4)
assert(Enum.slice([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 1..-2) == [2, 3, 4])
```

See also: alchem syntax streams, alchem syntax for, alchem doc Enum

## streams

stream[T]: a lazy sequence, consumed by Enum.

- Stream functions build a pipeline and run nothing; an Enum function (to_list, take, sum, each, reduce) pulls only what it needs.
- Streams may be infinite: Stream.iterate, Stream.cycle, Stream.from_index, Stream.repeatedly, Stream.unfold.
- File.stream!(path) reads a file lazily by line, or by chunks of bytes with a size; IO.stream() reads standard input.
- Stream.chunk_every(n) batches a stream for processing in chunks.
- Streams cannot be compared or sent to a process.

Example: lazy pipelines

```elixir
evens = Stream.iterate(0, &(&1 + 2))
assert(Enum.take(evens, 3) == [0, 2, 4])
batches = 1..1000000000
  |> Stream.map(&(&1 * 2))
  |> Stream.chunk_every(2)
  |> Enum.take(2)
assert(batches == [[2, 4], [6, 8]])
```

See also: alchem syntax ranges, alchem doc Stream, alchem doc Enum, alchem doc File

## sigils

~r regex, ~w words, ~s strings, ~D ~T ~N ~U dates and times.

- ~r/pattern/ is a regex checked at compile time (RE2 syntax); modifiers i, m, s, u may follow.
- ~w(one two) is a list of strings; ~s(text) is a string that may contain double quotes.
- ~D[2026-01-05] Date, ~T[13:04:05] Time, ~N[2026-01-05 13:04:05] NaiveDateTime, ~U[2026-01-05T13:04:05Z] DateTime.
- Delimiters may be / | " ' ( ) [ ] { } < >; the text has no escapes.
- ~s, ~w and ~r interpolate #{expression}; ~S never does. A ~r that interpolates is compiled when it runs rather than checked at compile time.
- String.replace and String.split accept a ~r in place of the text to look for.
- ~c(text) is the code points of the text as a list of integers; there are no charlists.
- Any other letter is a sigil the program defines: ~x(text)mods calls sigil_x(text, "mods"), a function taking two strings. A lower-case one interpolates.

Example: sigils

```elixir
assert(~w(red green blue) == ["red", "green", "blue"])
assert(Regex.run(~r/(\d+)-(\d+)/, "10-20") == some(["10-20", "10", "20"]))
assert("Hello" =~ ~r/^hello$/i)
assert(Date.add(~D[2026-12-31], 1) == ~D[2027-01-01])
assert(~s(say "hi") == "say \"hi\"")
```

Example: interpolation and regular expressions with String

```elixir
name = "ada"
assert(~s(hello #{name}) == "hello ada")
assert(~w(#{name} lovelace) == ["ada", "lovelace"])
assert(Regex.match?(~r/^#{name}$/i, "ADA"))
assert(~S(raw #{name}) == "raw \#{name}")
assert(String.replace("a1b22c", ~r/[0-9]+/, "-") == "a-b-c")
assert(String.split("a, b;c", ~r/[,;] */) == ["a", "b", "c"])
```

Example: code points and a sigil of your own

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  def sigil_p(text: string, modifiers: string): list[string] do
    parts = String.split(text, "/")
    if modifiers == "r" do
      Enum.reverse(parts)
    else
      parts
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(~c(hi!) == [104, 105, 33])
    assert(~p(usr/local/bin) == ["usr", "local", "bin"])
    root = "opt"
    assert(~p(#{root}/bin)r == ["bin", "opt"])
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax strings, alchem doc Regex, alchem doc Date

## modules

import "file.alc" brings another module's public functions and types.

- import takes a path relative to the importing file; call with the module's name: Math.double(3).
- def is public, defp private. Imported types are written Module.Type.
- Imports of a published package name a host path and version: import "github.com/owner/repo@v1.2.0/lib/math.alc"; versions are recorded in alchem.lock.
- Library modules (Enum, String, ...) need no import.

Example: two files

```elixir
# geometry.alc
defmodule Geometry do
  struct Size do
    width: integer
    height: integer
  end

  def area(size: Size): integer do
    size.width * size.height
  end
end

defmodule ShapesTest do
  import "geometry.alc"

  test "imported functions and types" do
    size = %Geometry.Size{width: 2, height: 3}
    assert(Geometry.area(size) == 6)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax program, alchem syntax extern, alchem syntax functions

## protocols

defprotocol declares functions; defimpl supplies them for one type.

- defprotocol Name do def function(value): type ... end declares functions without bodies.
- defimpl Name, for: Type do ... end defines every function of the protocol for one type: a builtin type, a struct or sum type from any module, or a generic type such as list[a]. The first parameter is the value and needs no annotation.
- A call Name.function(value, ...) is resolved when the program is compiled, from the type of its first argument. There is no dispatch while the program runs, so the type must be known where the call is written: it cannot be a type variable.
- A protocol is known by its own name in every module of the program, and a type may be given an implementation in any module.
- An implementation that lacks a function, or disagrees with the protocol on the number of arguments or the result type, is a compile error.

Example: one protocol, three types

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  struct Circle do
    radius: float
  end

  defprotocol Describe do
    def describe(value): string
  end

  defimpl Describe, for: integer do
    def describe(n): string do
      "the number #{n}"
    end
  end

  defimpl Describe, for: Circle do
    def describe(circle): string do
      "a circle of radius #{circle.radius}"
    end
  end

  defimpl Describe, for: list[a] do
    def describe(items): string do
      "a list of #{length(items)}"
    end
  end

  def main() do
    assert(Describe.describe(7) == "the number 7")
    assert(Describe.describe(%Circle{radius: 1.5}) == "a circle of radius 1.5")
    assert(Describe.describe(["a", "b"]) == "a list of 2")
    assert(Enum.map([1, 2], &Describe.describe(&1)) == ["the number 1", "the number 2"])
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax modules, alchem syntax structs, alchem syntax generics

## macros

defmacro defines a template; a call is replaced by the template with its arguments filled in.

- defmacro name(parameters) do quote do ... end end. Inside the quote, unquote(parameter) stands for the argument given at the call.
- Expansion happens before anything is typed and runs no code: it copies the quoted code and substitutes. What comes out is checked like any other code, and a problem is reported where the macro was called.
- A last parameter written do: name takes a do ... end block: name(arguments) do ... end. Only a macro takes a block.
- A macro whose template is one expression can be used as a value; one with several statements is used as a statement.
- An argument is put in wherever it is unquoted, so unquoting it twice evaluates it twice. Bind it once in the template to avoid that.
- A name the template binds is separate from the same name at the call, and a function the template calls is the one in the macro's own module.
- From another module a macro is called Module.name(...). A macro named __using__ holds function definitions, which use Module, option: value adds to the module that says so.

Example: a value, statements, and a block

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  defmacro square(value) do
    quote do
      unquote(value) * unquote(value)
    end
  end

  defmacro check(label, value) do
    quote do
      result = unquote(value)
      assert(result > 0)
      IO.puts("#{unquote(label)}: #{result}")
    end
  end

  defmacro unless_empty(items, do: body) do
    quote do
      if unquote(items) != [] do
        unquote(body)
      end
    end
  end

  def main() do
    result = 3
    assert(square(result + 1) == 16)
    check("doubled", result * 2)
    assert(result == 3)
    unless_empty([1, 2]) do
      IO.puts("has items")
    end
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax functions, alchem syntax modules, alchem syntax protocols

## nodes

Programs connect as nodes and their processes exchange messages, which are copied.

- Node.start(name, address, cookie) makes a program a node; Node.connect(address) connects it to another that knows the same cookie. With two arguments Node.start reads the cookie from ALCHEM_COOKIE.
- Process.register(pid, :name) names a process. Node.whereis(node, :name) finds it from another node as an option[pid[T]], where T comes from the annotation and must be the type it was registered with.
- Process.send to that handle copies the message across. A process handle inside a message crosses too, so the receiver can reply through it.
- A handle to a process of another node can be sent to and monitored: Process.monitor reports its exit as an event, or "noconnection" if its node is lost first. Process.alive tells whether its node is connected. Receiving, linking and awaiting need a process of this node. Node.monitor(node) reports a lost connection as an event whose reason is "nodedown" and the node's name.
- Stream.publish(:name, fn -> stream end) offers a stream to other nodes, and Node.stream(node, :name) reads it from one: elements are pulled a chunk at a time as they are consumed, so an endless or very large stream stays where it is.
- Only values that can be copied cross: no functions, streams, regular expressions, ports, tasks, agents or servers. The compiler checks this where a process is registered or looked up.
- Nodes that exchange a message type must agree on it: share the module that declares it.
- Connections are encrypted with TLS 1.3, and the cookie decides who may connect: each node proves it knows the cookie without sending it. Use a long random cookie, and keep it out of source control.
- Node.start(name, address, cookie, [encrypted: false]) turns encryption off, for a network you trust. Only nodes with the same setting connect, and a mismatch is reported on both sides.
- A send to another node returns once the message is written, not once it is received, and a full mailbox there delays and then drops messages.

Example: starting a node and naming a process

```elixir
started = Node.start("example", "127.0.0.1:0", "secret")
assert(started == ok({}) or started == error("this program is already a node"))
inbox: pid[tuple[atom, integer]] = Process.self(8)
Process.register(inbox, :example_inbox)
found: option[pid[tuple[atom, integer]]] = Process.whereis(:example_inbox)
sent = case found do
  some(named) -> Process.send(named, {:count, 3}, 100)
  none -> false
end
assert(sent)
assert_receive(inbox, {:count, 3})
Process.unregister(:example_inbox)
elsewhere: option[pid[tuple[atom, integer]]] = Node.whereis("other", :example_inbox, 50)
reached = case elsewhere do
  some(_) -> true
  none -> false
end
assert(not reached)
```

See also: alchem syntax processes, alchem doc Node, alchem doc Process

## extern

extern name(params): result = "package.Function" calls a Go function.

- The Alchem signature is checked against the Go one by alchem check.
- A Go (T, error) result is declared result[T, string]; (T, bool) is option[T].
- extern type Name = "*package.Type" names an opaque Go type; methods are "package.Type.Method" with the receiver first.
- require "module/path" "v1.2.3" adds a third-party Go module; "./dir.Function" refers to Go code beside the program.

Example: calling the Go standard library

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  extern shout(text: string): string = "strings.ToUpper"
  extern to_number(text: string): result[integer, string] = "strconv.Atoi"

  def main() do
    assert(shout("hello") == "HELLO")
    assert(to_number("42") == ok(42))
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax modules

## processes

Lightweight processes with typed mailboxes.

- pid[T] is a process whose mailbox carries T. Process.spawn(function, capacity) starts one; the function receives its own pid and returns an exit status.
- Process.self(capacity) is the current process; annotate it to fix the message type.
- Process.send(pid, message, timeout_ms) and Process.receive(self, timeout_ms) -> {arrived, message}.
- For state, prefer Server (request/reply), Agent (shared state) or Task (one result) over raw processes.
- Supervisor restarts failed children; Process.monitor and Process.link observe failures.

Example: send and receive

```elixir
parent: pid[string] = Process.self(8)
worker: pid[string] = Process.spawn(fn(self: pid[string]): integer do
  {_, text} = Process.receive(self, 1000)
  Process.send(parent, String.upcase(text), 1000)
  0
end, 8)
Process.send(worker, "hello", 1000)
assert(Process.receive(parent, 1000) == {true, "HELLO"})
```

Example: tasks and a server

```elixir
defmodule Example do
  type Request do
    add(amount: integer)
    read
  end

  def handle(total: integer, request: Request): tuple[integer, integer] do
    case request do
      Request.add(amount) -> {total + amount, total + amount}
      Request.read -> {total, total}
    end
  end

  def main() do
    squares = Task.async_stream(1..4, fn n -> n * n end) |> Enum.to_list()
    assert(squares == [1, 4, 9, 16])
    counter = Server.start(0, &handle)
    assert(Server.call(counter, Request.add(5), 1000) == ok(5))
    assert(Server.call(counter, Request.read, 1000) == ok(5))
    Server.stop(counter)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem doc Process, alchem doc Server, alchem doc Task, alchem doc Agent, alchem doc Supervisor

## tests

Test files end in _test.alc and are run by alchem test.

- test "name" do ... end defines a test; describe "group" do ... end groups tests and may nest.
- assert, refute, assert_raise, assert_in_delta and flunk are the assertions; a failed comparison shows both sides.
- on_exit(fn -> ... end) runs when the test ends, passed or failed; capture_io(fn -> ... end) returns what was printed; assert_receive(self, pattern) takes the first matching message from the test's own mailbox and binds the pattern's names; refute_receive(self, pattern) fails if one arrives. Both accept a when guard, a timeout in milliseconds and a failure message; assert_received and refute_received do not wait.
- setup do ... end runs before each test in its describe; setup_all once per file. A setup that ends in a struct passes it to tests written test "name", context do.
- @tag "slow" or @tag :slow marks the next test, @describetag the next describe and @moduletag the file; a tag may have a value, @tag kind: :db, owner: "ada". Run with --tag or --exclude, by name (kind) or by name and value (kind:db). @tag timeout: 500 gives one test its own limit in milliseconds, or :infinity; @tag :skip or skip: "reason" skips.
- alchem test --seed N repeats an order; --only text, --trace, --max-failures N, --cover and --cover-min P are the other flags.
- Test files are compiled and run in parallel, one per processor; --jobs 1 runs them one at a time. Their output is printed in the same order either way.

Example: a test file

```elixir
defmodule CartTest do
  struct Context do
    prices: list[integer]
  end

  setup do
    %Context{prices: [5, 10]}
  end

  describe "totals" do
    test "adds prices", context do
      assert(Enum.sum(context.prices) == 15)
    end

    describe "empty carts" do
      test "total nothing" do
        assert(Enum.sum(Enum.take([1], 0)) == 0)
      end
    end
  end

  @tag "slow"
  test "division by zero is reported" do
    assert_raise("division by zero", fn -> 1 / 0 end)
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax doctests, alchem doc Testing

## properties

check all pattern <- generator, ... do ... end checks a property on generated values.

- Generators come from the Gen module: Gen.integer(), Gen.integer(low, high), Gen.string(:alphanumeric), Gen.list_of(g), Gen.tuple(a, b), Gen.member_of(list), Gen.one_of(generators), Gen.map, Gen.filter, Gen.bind and more.
- Each generator may use what the ones before it bound: check all low <- Gen.integer(0, 9), high <- Gen.integer(low, 20) do ... end.
- Conditions between the generators drop the values that fail them, and max_runs: n changes how many values are tried, 100 unless ALCHEM_PROPERTY_RUNS says otherwise.
- Values grow with each run. When the body fails, the value is shrunk to the smallest one that still fails, and that one is reported with the failure.
- The values come from the test seed, so alchem test --seed N repeats a failure.

Example: a property

```elixir
defmodule ReverseTest do
  test "reversing twice gives the list back" do
    check all list <- Gen.list_of(Gen.integer()), max_runs: 50 do
      assert(Enum.reverse(Enum.reverse(list)) == list)
    end
  end

  test "a sorted list is ordered" do
    check all list <- Gen.list_of(Gen.integer(-5, 5)) do
      sorted = Enum.sort(list)
      assert(Enum.all?(Enum.zip(sorted, Enum.drop(sorted, 1)), fn {a, b} -> a <= b end))
    end
  end
end
```

See also: alchem syntax tests, alchem doc Gen

## doctests

doctest Module runs the alx> examples in a module's @doc strings.

- In @doc, a line alx> expression is run; the lines after it, up to a blank line, are the expected value.
- ...> continues the expression on the next line; an example without an expected value is only run.
- Examples in one @doc share bindings, top to bottom.
- The test file imports the module and says doctest Module.

Example: documented examples as tests

```elixir
# price.alc
defmodule Price do
  @doc """
  Adds tax at a percentage.

      alx> Price.with_tax(100, 20)
      120
      alx> net = 50
      alx> Price.with_tax(net, 10)
      55
  """
  def with_tax(net: integer, percent: integer): integer do
    net + net * percent / 100
  end
end

defmodule PriceTest do
  import "price.alc"
  doctest Price
end
```

See also: alchem syntax comments, alchem syntax tests
